cards.explanation: The answer is a mocker. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says it plainly: “…a mocker does not listen to rebuke.” The mocker is the one who does not listen. Set beside him is the wise son who heeds his father's discipline.

The answer is False. The verse says the desire of the faithless is violence, and peace isn't in it. Across from that, a man enjoys good things from the fruit of his lips. Solomon sets the two statements side by side, friends.

The answer is guarding his mouth. “He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin.” Solomon sets two men side by side. One guards his mouth and protects his life, and the other opens his lips and invites his own ruin. Keep that mouth on a short leash, friends.
The answer is satisfied. The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is “fully satisfied.” The diligent person doesn't just get by, he gets full. That's a good place to end up.

The answer is that wickedness undermines him. “Righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner.” Righteousness does the guarding, and wickedness does the undermining. So the one who gets guarded is the man of integrity. Picture a cookie box with the bottom already gone.

The answer is True. One pretends to be rich but has nothing, and another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. Solomon is pointing out that what you see on the outside doesn't always match what's in the pockets. Looks can be fooling, friends.
The answer is no threat. Riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat. Solomon doesn't say which life is easier, he just lays the two side by side. Let him make the point, friends.
The answer is False. The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished. It goes out. Solomon sets a bright light next to a dark one.

The answer is advice. “Arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised.” Solomon says wisdom is with the well-advised, the people who take advice. Arrogance, on the other hand, leads only to strife. So wisdom shows up where advice is welcome.

The answer is dwindle. “Dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied.” Dishonest wealth is the one that dwindles. What is earned through hard work is the part that gets multiplied. So one kind of wealth shrinks and the other grows.

The answer is True. Verse 12 says, “Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.” Solomon names both the sick heart and the tree of life. The second half is the part this card asked about.

The answer is True. Solomon says the one who despises instruction will pay the penalty, but the one who respects a command will be rewarded. Following the instructions has a payoff, friends. Fewer leftover screws, I'd say.
The answer is the snares of death. The teaching of the wise is “…a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death.” A snare is a trap. The teaching turns a person away from it.

The answer is False. A fool doesn't keep his folly hidden, he displays it. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but the fool shows his folly right out in the open. No apron big enough to cover that.

The answer is healing. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing. Solomon puts the two messengers side by side. The faithful one brings healing, and that's a fine thing to carry, friends.

The answer is honored. Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored. Taking correction ends in honor. That's a good trade for a little humility, friends.
The answer is turning from evil. Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is detestable to fools. That's a hard thing to read. Fools don't want to turn from it.

The answer is that he will be destroyed. He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed. Who you walk with matters. It's worth picking your walking buddies carefully, friends.
The answer is True. Disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous. Solomon sets the two paths side by side. Disaster chases one, and the other gets a reward.

The answer is righteous. “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is passed to the righteous.” The sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous, and that's the whole answer. The good man, meanwhile, leaves an inheritance to his children's children. Not the owner's plan, I bet.

The answer is a lack of justice. “Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away.” The food was there, and it still got swept away. Solomon names the cause plainly: without justice. So the lack of justice is what takes the abundance.

The answer is disciplines. He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently. Solomon links love with the diligence of discipline. It's a heavy one to read, friends, and he says it plain.

The answer is False. Solomon says, “A righteous man eats to his heart’s content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty.” The stomach of the wicked is empty, not full. The righteous man is the one who eats to his heart's content.
